evidence_set: Unweighted counts: 4,631 of 19,549 men and 3,121 of 19,263 women with an age at first drink in Table 1 have a time from first drink to dependence, 23.7% and 16.2% (editors' arithmetic; ratio 1.46); the first-drink counts total 38,812, more than the 38,309 lifetime drinkers analysed in Table 2, and the dependence counts total 7,752, fewer than the 8,564 people with dependence analysed in Table 2 (study card reporting issue), so the shares are approximate. For time from first drink to dependence, Table 1 marks no gender difference as significant in the cohorts born 1974–1983 (men 2.8, women 3.1 years), 1944–1953 (7.9, 8.6) and 1934–1943 (10.4, 11.8).

evidence_set: As summarized (Kaskutas et al., 2005): women were randomized to a women-only day programme with gender-specific content or to one of three mixed-gender day programmes (two community-based, one hospital-based); the only significant outcome differences were between the women-only and the hospital-based programme, which had higher total abstinence during follow-up and cost twice as much per week, so the women-only programme did not differ significantly from the two community-based programmes; the sample was small; the review, citing the trial, says the findings suggest that women may be equally well served by high-quality mixed-gender and women-only day programmes.

As summarized: nicotine dependence is the exception to the pattern of no gender difference, with worse outcomes in women; nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study; varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (14,389 people, 51% women), as well in both sexes against placebo but with greater benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; there is some evidence that with naltrexone for smoking, men reduced smoking more and women gained less weight. For other medicines, gender differences were not consistently shown: women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence; a poorer response in women has not been reported in trials of disulfiram for alcohol dependence, perhaps because women were badly under-represented (for example 1.2%); naltrexone for alcohol dependence gave mixed findings (men better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no significant difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, where buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.

evidence_set: Table 1 values among people who use cocaine, taking the shorter window and powder over crack as the review did, run 23.5% to 87% (simultaneous alcohol), 9.3% to 76.5% (simultaneous cannabis), 34.9% to 96.5% (concurrent alcohol; Table 1's lifetime figures, left out by that rule, reach 98.3%) and 43.2% to 93.7% (concurrent cannabis). Editors' calculation (AI reader 288, agreeing with second reader 278's): DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling on the logit scale of these values, with the review's rules (shorter window, powder over crack), gives 37.9% (95% CI 19.7–60.3%) from 7 sources for simultaneous cannabis and 77.0% (62.1–87.2%) from 11 for concurrent alcohol, matching the printed 38% and 77%, but 70.1% (46.1–86.5%) from 8 for simultaneous alcohol and 66.5% (49.5–80.1%) from 8 for concurrent cannabis, against the printed 74% and 64%.
